heading: C06–C16 | Ethical hacking depends on authorization, boundaries and handling of results

body.text: The same person using the same tools and vulnerability-verification method may perform legitimate security testing or violate rules and potentially laws, depending on authorization, purpose and conduct.
The useful framework goes beyond labeling white hats good and black hats bad: security testing needs valid authority, operational control, verifiable evidence and accountability.
Keep five principles in view:

items: Authorization: who has authority to permit the test, and who may perform it?
Scope: which assets, systems and data may be tested?
Rules of engagement, or ROE: which actions are permitted, when may testing occur, and when must it stop?
Evidence: how can the team demonstrate the weakness and a controlled testing process?
Remediation: how do findings lead to fixes, lower risk and verification?

body.text: This approach uses the planning, testing, assessment and reporting guidance in NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, together with OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK and Taiwanese and US industry requirements.

This chapter retains the C06–C16 concept identifiers and mainly relates to M01-03, Ethical Hacking, Authorization and Rules of Engagement. Formal sub-identifiers for C12 and C13 and cross-chapter details for C16 remain unverified. These concept identifiers do not represent newly published course lessons.

body.text: One continuing scenario connects the concepts.

Scenario: a large Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer hires a Silicon Valley cybersecurity company to assess its customer-design data exchange platform. The platform exchanges necessary information with a supply-chain financing system at an FSC-regulated bank.
This is a hypothetical teaching scenario, not a claim that any particular company has a vulnerability.

heading: 2 | C06: Why ethical hacking is needed

body.text: 1. Assess defenses from an attacker’s perspective
Imagine that you manage information security at a semiconductor company.
The company has purchased firewalls, endpoint protection and identity services and established dozens of security policies.
Management asks:
“Are we actually secure?”
You might answer:
“We have firewalls and multifactor authentication, and we comply with our information-security policies.”
This does not adequately demonstrate resistance to real attacks.
The reason is straightforward:
The existence of a control does not establish its effectiveness.
For example, a system may require login while its API still lets an engineer obtain another customer’s confidential design files.
Ethical hacking addresses this gap in evidence.
Ethical hacking uses techniques an attacker might employ, under appropriate authorization and controls, to identify and verify weaknesses and improve organizational defenses.
2. Three different security activities

rows: Are specified policies and requirements followed?
Review documents, controls and execution evidence
Can weaknesses be exploited, and with what impact?
Controlled exploitation verification and risk analysis

body.text: These activities overlap but do not replace one another.
Chapter 4 of NIST SP 800-115 addresses target identification and analysis. Chapter 5 addresses vulnerability-validation techniques, including penetration testing to verify exploitability.
3. Using OWASP and MITRE ATT&CK
Suppose the semiconductor platform exposes an API:
`GET /api/designs/1234`
A researcher suspects that changing the file identifier might expose another customer’s designs.
Two bodies of knowledge can help in different ways.
OWASP identifies application controls that should be checked.
API1 in the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 is Broken Object Level Authorization, or BOLA.
Whenever an API uses an object identifier to access data, it must verify whether the current user may perform the requested operation on that object.
MITRE ATT&CK helps describe how real adversaries operate.
For example, T1190, Exploit Public-Facing Application, describes exploiting weaknesses in externally accessible services to gain initial access.
Their perspectives differ:

body.name: securityframeworks
body.caption: OWASP and MITRE ATT&CK: complementary perspectives
body.description: These are parallel perspectives. NIST SP 800-115 adds assessment planning, execution, evidence and reporting. An ATT&CK identifier does not authorize a test.

items.title: OWASP
items.body:
Starts with application weaknesses and security controls
What should be tested, verified and improved?

items.title: MITRE ATT&CK
items.body:
Starts with observed adversary behavior
How do attackers act, and can defenses detect them?

body.text: NIST SP 800-115 adds methods for planning and executing tests, preserving evidence and reporting results.
C06 focuses on the trustworthy, actionable security evidence delivered to an organization, rather than counting systems compromised.
1. A company engagement does not authorize testing every company system
Return to the semiconductor scenario.
Suppose the engagement letter says only:
“Please assist with an information-security penetration test.”
This indicates an intention to collaborate but leaves important operational questions unanswered.
For example, the researcher may not know:

items: May the production environment be tested?
Does permission include infrastructure managed by a cloud provider?
May the team access other customers’ information?
May it attempt to change manufacturing-equipment parameters?

body.text: Professional testing needs authorization translated into explicit operational permissions.
NIST defines ROE as rules established before testing that authorize the team to perform specifically defined activities.
2. Two meanings of authorization
Keep the following distinction when studying more advanced security topics.

rows: An asset owner or appropriate authority permits specified security testing
The data and functions that the system permits a user to access

body.text: A researcher may be authorized by the semiconductor company to test its customer-data platform for access-control weaknesses.
That testing permission can be valid even though the purpose is to determine whether the application’s access authorization can be bypassed.
OWASP WSTG-ATHZ-02 addresses authorization-bypass testing, including horizontal access between users with the same privileges and vertical access between different roles.
3. Unauthorized access under Taiwanese and US law
Taiwan: Criminal Code Articles 358–360.

Article 358 addresses intrusion without justification using another person’s credentials, defeating computer protections or exploiting a system weakness. Article 359 addresses obtaining, deleting or altering another person’s electromagnetic records without justification and causing damage. Article 360 addresses interference without justification with another person’s computer through programs or other electromagnetic means and resulting damage.
The provisions have different elements; assess actual conduct against each applicable provision.
United States: the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, or CFAA, 18 U.S.C. §1030.
Subsection (a)(2) covers specified unauthorized or excessive access that obtains information. Subsection (a)(5) addresses specified conduct causing computer damage without authorization.

The DOJ’s 2022 CFAA charging policy directs prosecutors not to charge conduct meeting its definition of good-faith security research. It is a federal prosecution policy, not an unlimited grant of testing permission.
4. Why document authorization in writing?
Written documents identify the authorizer, tester, targets, validity period, permitted activities and responsibilities.
Common documents include an authorization letter, statement of work or SOW, ROE and a nondisclosure agreement or NDA.
They serve different purposes: an NDA governs confidentiality, an SOW defines deliverables, ROE governs testing operations, and appropriate written authorization establishes clear testing permission.
C07: the person commissioning a test must have corresponding authority over the target assets. Permission to test one asset does not extend automatically to every connected asset.

heading: 4 | C08: Making scope and ROE operational

body.text: 1. Scope defines the testing boundary; ROE defines operating rules
Suppose a bank authorizes testing only in its online-banking test environment.
This defines the scope.
The researcher still needs answers to questions such as:
“At what times may we test? What request rate is allowed? May we verify privilege escalation? Who can require us to stop if the system behaves abnormally?”
These belong in the ROE.
NIST SP 800-115 allows ROE to include both scope and operating rules. Separating scope here helps explain and manage their different functions.
2. Six practical control areas for ROE

Appendix B of NIST SP 800-115 includes objectives, scope, risks, personnel, schedule, communications, target systems, permitted and prohibited actions, data handling, reporting and signatures. The following table groups these into six practical areas.

rows: Authorizer, testing team, accountable managers, signatures and validity period
Included and excluded domains, IPs, APIs, cloud accounts, data and equipment
Permitted tools and verification methods, prohibited actions and operating limits
Testing windows, load limits, stop conditions and recovery procedures
SOC, system owners, emergency contacts and escalation
Logs, sensitive-data handling, findings, remediation and retesting

body.text: 3. Why semiconductor equipment cannot all be tested like general IT
The following historical incident makes the risk concrete.

Appendix C.3.4 of NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology Security, records a ping sweep on an industrial-control network that halted a chip-manufacturing control system and destroyed approximately US$50,000 worth of wafers. It also records a separate industrial-network probing incident that caused unexpected movement of a robotic arm.
A probe considered relatively low risk in an ordinary IT network can have very different consequences in operational technology, or OT.

body.name: itotrisks
body.caption: Security testing carries different risks
body.description: Requirements depend on actual assets and risks, rather than imposing identical restrictions on every IT or OT system. The comparison does not imply that OT can ignore data security or recovery.

items.title: Enterprise IT systems
items.body:
Office networks, websites and general applications
Key concerns: service availability, data security and recovery

items.title: Fab OT systems
items.body:
Manufacturing equipment, control systems and process networks
Additional concerns: equipment safety, process stability and physical loss

body.text: SEMI E187, Specification for Cybersecurity of Fab Equipment, addresses operating-system support, network security, endpoint protection and security monitoring. Its public scope primarily covers equipment computing devices running Windows or Linux; it does not cover all PLCs, SCADA systems or associated sensor and actuator devices.
Taiwan also has a semiconductor-equipment cybersecurity assessment and certification scheme based on SEMI E187.
Combining NIST SP 800-82’s OT risk guidance with SEMI E187’s equipment-security requirements suggests ROE such as:

Assess safety impacts before testing production equipment. Prefer passive monitoring, offline analysis or a validated test environment. Active testing of production equipment requires additional approval, stop conditions and recovery measures.
This is a risk-based engineering design derived from the references, not a claim that SEMI E187 prescribes identical testing procedures for every device.
C08: ROE is an operational mechanism for controlling testing conduct, beyond its role as documentation.

heading: 5 | C09–C13: Distinguish conduct, purpose and ability

body.text: These five terms belong together because they describe different classification dimensions.
C09 | White hat
A white-hat researcher or tester acts under appropriate authorization, aims to improve security and follows agreed testing rules.
Suppose a Silicon Valley company hires a researcher to assess its product APIs.
The researcher obtains written permission, uses company-provided test accounts, checks for authorization bypass, reports findings and assists with retesting.
This is typical white-hat conduct.
The key question concerns compliance with authorization, scope and purpose, rather than how technically impressive the researcher is.
Practical reference: NIST SP 800-115 Chapters 6–8 address planning, execution, reporting and mitigation activities.
C10 | Grey hat
Grey hat commonly describes security exploration without clear malicious intent but without authorization or full adherence to testing rules.
For example, a researcher suspects a weakness in a bank website.
Without permission, the researcher accesses other customers’ data and later privately tells the bank, “I found a vulnerability for you.”
An initial intention to improve security does not automatically grant testing permission.
Distinguish three propositions:

rows: The researcher wants to help improve security
Legality depends on the applicable law and facts

body.text: The DOJ’s 2022 CFAA policy illustrates the distinction between motivation, conduct, charging policy and legal authorization.
C11 | Black hat
Black hat commonly describes unauthorized intrusion with theft, extortion, destruction or another malicious purpose.
For example, an attacker obtains information through a semiconductor supply-chain entry point and sells confidential technical documents to a third party.
The central issues include unauthorized access and improper acquisition of information.
In Taiwan, assess the conduct against Criminal Code Articles 358–360 and, when the information meets the statutory definition, relevant Trade Secrets Act provisions.
C12 | Blue hat
This term has no fully consistent meaning across sources.
Some educational sources use blue hat for external experts invited to test products before release; others use it for attackers motivated by revenge.

The [ESET glossary](https://help.eset.com/glossary/en-US/hacker.html) uses the invited-consultant meaning. Table 7 of the [ORE Catapult 2025 report](https://cms.ore.catapult.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/PN844-RPT-006_WP4-Cybersecurity-and-Autonomous-Systems-Report_Rev2.pdf) records both revenge-motivated and invited-testing meanings. These are source-specific classifications, not a uniform official CEH legal or identity category.
Microsoft also runs a security-research event called BlueHat. Attendance does not assign a fixed legal or technical hacker category to its participants.
For a CEH question containing blue hat, interpret the scenario and assigned materials rather than deciding solely from the color.
C13 | Script kiddie: limited experience and reliance on ready-made tools
Script kiddie commonly describes a person with limited technical understanding who primarily uses tools or programs developed by others.
Technical ability and authorization are different dimensions.
A beginner using Nmap in an authorized lab may be learning security testing appropriately. An experienced engineer intruding without permission may still act improperly.
The term primarily describes ability or tool use; it does not independently determine legality.
A more precise classification model
Use three independent dimensions to describe conduct:

headers: No valid authorization or outside scope
rows: Malicious activity not permitted by the engagement falls outside its authorization

body.text: Analyze technical ability separately from this purpose-and-authorization matrix.
CEH introduces white, grey and black hats, while enterprise governance needs descriptions of actual conduct, permissions, purpose and evidence rather than color labels alone.
Penetration testing involves more than simply trying to break in.
It establishes a repeatable process under predefined safety conditions to verify weaknesses, analyze potential impacts and provide evidence for improvement.
1. The evidence distinction between scanning and penetration testing
Suppose a scanner reports that a web server uses a component version associated with a known vulnerability.
This is an important clue but does not establish that exploitation will succeed.
The system might have a backported fix without a changed version string, the weakness might depend on a particular configuration, or the necessary preconditions might be absent.
Verification is therefore necessary.

body.name: validationevidence
body.caption: From a potential weakness to verified improvement
body.description: Arrows show the assessment and remediation workflow. Controlled verification uses authorized assets and test data; greater damage or collecting real customer data is not required as proof.

items.title: Observe a potential weakness
items.body: Scanning, configuration analysis or source review

items.title: Form a testable hypothesis
items.body: Can this weakness be exploited under the specified conditions?

items.title: Perform controlled verification
items.body: Use authorized assets and test data, doing enough to confirm the weakness

items.title: Record observations and limits
items.body: Evidence, impact, test conditions and untested scope

items.title: Remediate and retest
items.body: Confirm closure while legitimate business operations remain functional

body.text: The reasoning resembles scientific work: observation, hypothesis, experiment, evidence, conclusion and reproducibility.
Penetration testing adds a critical constraint: the verification activity itself must remain within risk limits.
2. Penetration-testing phases in NIST SP 800-115
Section 5.2 describes Planning, Discovery, Attack and Reporting. Reporting can run throughout the process rather than beginning only after all technical work ends.

rows: Define objectives, authorization, ROE and risks
Understand systems, services and potential weaknesses
Analyze impacts, remediation priorities and limitations

body.text: 3. Advanced scenario: verify BOLA in a design-data platform
Suppose the testing team controls two accounts:
Account A belongs to test customer A; account B belongs to test customer B.
Each owns an artificial design document containing no real trade secrets.
The verification question is:
Can account A read account B’s test document without access authorization?
This is a specific, testable security hypothesis.
OWASP WSTG-ATHZ-02 describes horizontal authorization testing between different users at the same privilege level.
If A can read B’s test data, the team has evidence of the weakness. It need not download all real customers’ documents.
A further question is whether the server checks permission on every data access or only once at login.
This affects remediation.
The underlying problem may be missing object-level authorization in the backend API rather than in the frontend page.
4. Assessing penetration-test quality
A conceptual model for research and enterprise delivery is:
Testing value ≈ verifiable, actionable security evidence ÷ (testing cost and additional risk introduced)
This is a reasoning aid, not an official NIST calculation.
A useful report explains the necessary conditions, observed impact, evidence, remediation direction and how to verify the fix.
C14: evaluate testing by verifiable risk findings and effective improvement rather than the damage it causes.

heading: 7 | C15: Disclosure, confidentiality and research responsibility

body.text: 1. Discovering a weakness does not grant permission to publish everything
Suppose a researcher discovers a serious weakness in a Taiwanese semiconductor company’s system.
It might let one customer read another customer’s unpublished chip designs.
Owning the technical discovery does not grant ownership of, disposal rights over or publication rights to customer documents.
Research must manage both vulnerability details and sensitive information encountered during testing.
2. Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure, or CVD
CVD means coordinated vulnerability disclosure.
Researchers report to an appropriate security contact so the vendor, researcher and stakeholders can coordinate verification, remediation, notification and publication timing.

OWASP’s Vulnerability Disclosure Cheat Sheet recommends lawful, authorized testing, respect for privacy, sufficient verification and reproduction information, and avoiding demands for payment as a disclosure condition outside established reward schemes.
A practical finding report might contain:

rows: Test accounts A and B and specified data
Possible failure of isolation between customers
Redacted requests, responses and access logs
Enforce object-level authorization in the backend
A cannot obtain B’s data, while permitted access remains functional

body.text: OWASP API1:2023 specifically calls for object-level authorization checks in data-access operations involving object IDs supplied by clients.
3. Legal connection for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry
Article 2 of the Trade Secrets Act identifies secrecy, economic value arising from secrecy, and reasonable secrecy measures as the core requirements.

External assessments should use data classification, minimum necessary access, confidentiality agreements, evidence preservation and controlled delivery to limit exposure of sensitive technical information.
4. Vulnerability-reporting programs at Silicon Valley companies
Technology companies commonly define permitted assets and activities through a Vulnerability Disclosure Policy, or VDP, or a bug-bounty program.
OWASP recommends clear scope, testing rules, reporting methods and applicable safe-harbor conditions. A `security.txt` file following RFC 9116 can help researchers find the reporting contact.
A bug-bounty invitation has specific conditions and does not authorize unrestricted testing of every company system.
5. Financial-sector information protection and oversight

Article 24 of Taiwan’s banking internal-control rules requires a dedicated information-security unit for applicable institutions. Article 25 addresses security planning, risk control and incident notification and response responsibilities.

Institutions commissioning external penetration tests can translate these responsibilities into contractor procedures, protection of sensitive customer data, incident notification and remediation tracking.

The Bankers Association announced its financial-institution ICT and service supply-chain risk-management rules on March 5, 2026; the attachment version is v2026.2.13. The announcement date and document-version date have different meanings. These self-regulatory rules are an additional reference for financial-sector supply-chain governance.
C15: handling evidence, communicating risk and completing remediation determine whether a discovery improves security.

heading: 8 | C16: Distinguish attack purpose from testing purpose

body.text: CEH questions sometimes contrast ethical hacking with DoS, data theft and distributing malware.
The question usually concerns primary purpose rather than technical sophistication.
1. Describing adversary behavior with MITRE ATT&CK

rows: Unauthorized access, privilege escalation and related effects

body.text: These references use the official MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise technique pages.
Keep the following distinction:
ATT&CK describes adversary behavior and techniques. It does not determine whether a particular test has permission.
A research team may simulate selected techniques under controlled conditions to assess defenses, but authorization and ROE determine whether it may do so.
2. A banking DDoS scenario
Suppose a bank wants to establish whether online banking can withstand large volumes of malicious requests.
That objective can be legitimate security validation.
Directly generating large attack traffic against production banking could, however, stop customer transactions, create serious operational risk and exceed authorization.
First identify the defense capability that needs validation.
Examples include detection by a traffic-scrubbing service, rate limits, response procedures or capacity under a specified traffic scenario.
Then select a simulated environment, controlled load or approved provider testing mechanism according to risk and ROE.
Article 25 of Taiwan’s banking internal-control rules assigns CIA oversight and incident notification and response to the dedicated security unit, consistent with these risk-control objectives.
3. A decision model for legitimate security testing

body.name: authorizationgates
body.caption: Authorization and risk gates for security testing
body.description: A practical model derived from NIST SP 800-115 and OWASP disclosure principles, not a legal-liability test. Both negative branches stop. Only the branch passing both gates proceeds to controlled verification and closure.

items.title: Propose a testing activity
items.body: State the control and purpose to be assessed

items.title: Is valid authorization in place?
items.body: Authorizer, validity period, tester and assets

items.title: No: do not perform it as an authorized test
items.body: Stop; obtain appropriate authorization and reassess

items.title: Yes: review the activity and risk
items.body: Does it comply with scope, ROE and risk limits?

items.title: No: stop and request an authorization change
items.body: This branch does not proceed to execution or closure

items.title: Yes: perform controlled verification and preserve evidence
items.body: Continue observing stop conditions and data-handling rules

items.title: Report, remediate, retest and close
items.body: Record observations, limits, remediation and acceptance evidence

body.text: The table translates the cited requirements into governance recommendations. Testing focus and ROE design are risk-based engineering choices, not identical mandatory checklists prescribed by every reference.
Advanced question: why is testing a governance issue?
Penetration testing is often viewed primarily as technical work.

When it crosses departments, cloud providers, external consultants, financial data or manufacturing equipment, the team must determine who can authorize it, accept risk, stop work and own remediation.
Professional testing therefore needs three coordinated layers:

rows: Does the weakness exist, and how can it be verified?
OWASP WSTG, scanning and controlled tests
ROE, stop conditions, SOC and incident response
Who can approve, oversee and accept responsibility?
Authorization, risk management, audit and compliance

body.text: The shared objective is to keep potentially destructive technical activity within an authorized, auditable and controllable execution boundary.
The following primary documents support further reading and citation.

rows: Industry standard and associated certification scheme
Website announcement February 5, 2026; attachment filename includes 1150107

body.text: Version matters: this chapter uses the final NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3. Revision 4 has a public draft, which is not treated here as a final standard. OWASP WSTG’s stable release is v4.2, while its development documentation continues to change.
Try reasoning independently before consulting references. These questions combine C06–C16.
Scenario:
A Taiwanese semiconductor-equipment company hires a US security company to assess its supply-chain platform. The team has written authorization for a specified test environment.
The following events occur:
A. An engineer uses OWASP methods and finds that one test account may read another account’s test document.
B. The engineer suspects the same weakness exists in production and logs into production to verify it, although production is outside the authorized scope.
C. The engineer discovers a connection between the equipment-management and office networks and decides to actively scan equipment controllers, although the ROE does not permit OT testing.
D. The team uses only artificial test data, records complete evidence, reports to the company’s security owner and recommends remediation.

E. Another researcher suspects a weakness in a Taiwanese bank’s transaction platform, attempts to access other customers’ transaction records without permission, and later says the purpose was to help.
Answer the following:

items: 1. Classification: which A–E activities comply with valid authorization and testing boundaries, which require new approval, and which resemble typical white-hat or grey-hat scenarios?
2. Standards: how should the different roles of NIST SP 800-82 and SEMI E187 inform a redesigned procedure for the OT risk in C?
3. Engineering: which OWASP testing concept applies to A? How might the observed behavior map to ATT&CK, and why do the two frameworks not replace one another?
4. Law and governance: if B’s production system contains a US company’s customer data and E’s bank is in Taiwan, which laws, authorization documents and industry rules would you examine first?
5. Research method: how would you design minimum sufficient validation to establish the weakness while limiting disclosure, equipment anomalies and effects on third parties?

body.text: The central capability is translating security-testing techniques into an authorized, risk-limited engineering process that produces trustworthy evidence and improves systems. This connects C06–C16 with cybersecurity research and operational governance.
